history.action: route plan -> implement -> review -> qa (model, confidence 88)

validated_work_order.confidence_rationale: Every claim in the ticket was verified in the code rather than taken on trust: the three cleanup findings each had exactly zero external consumers on a repo-wide grep, the hang path was traced from CustomReport.tsx's isComplexCategoryCondition through custom-spreadsheet.ts:93 and grouped-spreadsheet.ts:45 to budgetDataQuery.ts:249/261, and the cost curve that sets the threshold was measured on this runner rather than estimated. The design question the ticket flags - which way the bound fails - was settled by walking both operators against both sides of the query, and the trap (a match-everything regex inverts doesNotContain into the money-losing direction) is named with the code shape that avoids it. What is left uncertain is only how much of AC-1 a QA run on the demo budget can actually observe, which is why AC-8 carries the hard, falsifiable form of the same claim and AC-1 is written to what a live browser can see.
validated_work_order.understanding: A category filter value like `%%%%%%Z` typed into a Custom or Grouped report freezes the browser's main thread for minutes. The path is synchronous and inside React's render: CustomReport.tsx marks a `category` + `contains/doesNotContain/matches/hasTags` condition as `isComplexCategoryCondition`, which routes the report through `createCustomSpreadsheet`, whose body calls `narrowCategoriesByConditions` -> `filterCategoriesByConditions` -> `likePatternToRegex('%' + value + '%')` once per category per condition, every render. Each `%` compiles to `.*`, so the value becomes `.*` x 8 followed by `Z`, and `.test()` against a category name backtracks over the partitions of that name. The cost is in `.test()`, not in compilation - I measured compilation at <=0.06 ms in every case, which is why the epic's memoisation note is right and why the bound is the whole fix. `unicodeLike` (the sqlite `UNICODE_LIKE` scalar, reached from every `contains` rule through aql/compiler.ts:735) goes through the same function and already memoises through an LRU, so it does not need a second bound and does not need its own memoisation. The bound belongs in `likePatternToRegex` and must be expressible in its return type, because a caller that cannot see a refusal will silently compile the catastrophic regex. It must fail OPEN: a refusal keeps every category, on both operators - including `doesNotContain`, which is the trap, because a refusal represented as a match-everything regex negates to 'drop everything' and drops every category the query fetched. The ticket also carries three cleanup findings in the same two files; I verified all three (zero external consumers each).
validated_work_order.root_cause: Unbounded wildcard expansion in the LIKE-pattern compiler. `likePatternToRegex` translates every unescaped `%` into `.*` with no limit, and the regex engine backtracks exponentially (~7x per additional wildcard) over the partitions of the subject string on `.test()`. The report axis runs that `.test()` once per category per condition on every render, so a value with six `%` is 8 wildcards against every category name. The cost is in matching, not compiling: compilation stayed at <=0.06 ms for every pattern I measured, so caching the regex (which `unicodeLike` already does) cannot fix it and no memoisation is warranted.
validated_work_order.approach:
Make `likePatternToRegex` return `RegExp | null`, refusing a pattern that is over-long or over-wildcarded, and teach its two consumers to treat `null` as 'matches every string' so the failure direction is open everywhere.

1. The bound, in `likePattern.ts` only. Two module-private constants and one counting pass in the existing compile loop: `MAX_PATTERN_LENGTH = 256` (the same number, and the same precedent, as the `matches` guard at budgetDataQuery.ts:274-278) and `MAX_UNESCAPED_WILDCARDS = 4`. Count only unescaped `%` and `?` - a `\%` compiles to a literal and adds no `.*`. Refuse by returning `null` before `new RegExp(...)` is ever constructed. The wildcard count, not the length, is what carries AC-1: six `%` is an eight-character pattern that no length cap would catch.

2. Why 4, computed rather than guessed. I re-measured the epic's curve on this runner (300 categories, ~45-character names, value = `%`x n + 'Z', pattern = `'%' + value + '%'`):

| wildcards in pattern | value | 300 categories | per category |
|---|---|---|---|
| 3 | `%Z` | 8.5 ms | 0.03 ms |
| 4 | `%%Z` | 105 ms | 0.35 ms |
| 5 | `%%%Z` | 1.02 s | 3.4 ms |
| 6 | `%%%%Z` | 10.2 s | 34 ms |
| 7 | `%%%%%Z` | 84 s | 281 ms |

Compile time was <=0.06 ms in every row. Six `%` (AC-1's value) is an 8-wildcard pattern and is not in this table. A cap of 4 leaves the accepted region at <=105 ms across 300 categories and cuts everything from 1 s upward; a cap of 5 would admit a 1 s render, a cap of 6 a 10 s one. The cap also preserves the pinned existing behaviour: `contains '%'` and `contains '?'` compile to 3-wildcard patterns and still match everything.

3. Why `RegExp | null` and not a match-everything regex. THE TRAP: `contains` keeps a category when the regex matches and `doesNotContain` keeps it when the regex does NOT match. Returning `/^[\s\S]*$/i` for a refusal therefore fails OPEN for `contains` and fails CLOSED for `doesNotContain` - it drops every category, which is the money-losing direction AC-3 exists to prevent. `null` forces each call site to make the decision explicitly, and TypeScript makes the compiler refuse to let a future consumer forget.

THE RULE, as it must appear in the code: a refused pattern is treated as matching every string, and every consumer of a refusal KEEPS every category - including the `doesNotContain` branch, which must return `true` on a refusal rather than negating a match-everything result.

WORKED EXAMPLES (computed, not asserted), value `%%%%%%Z`, 8 unescaped wildcards, refused:
- `contains`: axis keeps all N categories. Query side: `$like` -> `UNICODE_LIKE` returns 1 for every row -> every transaction returned. Axis == result set; totals unchanged.
- `doesNotContain`: axis keeps all N categories (NOT zero). Query side: `$notlike` -> `NOT 1` -> no transactions returned. Axis is strictly WIDER than the result set; at worst a kept category shows 0.00 under 'Show empty rows'.

INVARIANT, which is the whole safety argument and what QA should check: for any refused pattern and any budget, the set of categories the axis renders is a SUPERSET of the categories present in the query's result set - equivalently, no category the query fetched loses its row, and no money leaves a total because a value was too long. The bound cannot violate it, because every refusal path returns 'keep'.

4. `unicodeLike` treats a refusal as a match and returns 1. That keeps the invariant on the query side too: under `$like` the query returns everything (equal to the axis) and under `$notlike` it returns nothing (a subset of the axis). One mechanical change it forces: the cache's `if (!cachedRegExp)` must become an `=== undefined` sentinel, because a cached `null` is falsy and would otherwise re-run the compile for every row.

5. The three cleanups ride along: unexport `REGEX_SPECIAL` (repo-wide grep finds no consumer outside its own module), unexport `canNarrowAxisByConditions` (exported, one caller at line 137 of the same file) with the reason recorded next to it, and delete the `// ? added here` scar while keeping the branch's explanatory comment.

files.change: Add two module-private constants - `MAX_PATTERN_LENGTH = 256` and `MAX_UNESCAPED_WILDCARDS = 4`, both unexported - and change the signature to `export function likePatternToRegex(pattern: string): RegExp | null`. Return `null` when `pattern.length > MAX_PATTERN_LENGTH` before compiling anything. Inside the existing while loop, keep a `wildcards` counter incremented only on the unescaped `%` (`regexStr += '.*'`) and unescaped `?` (`regexStr += '.'`) branches - NOT on the escaped-wildcard branch, where `\%` compiles to a literal - and return `null` when the count exceeds `MAX_UNESCAPED_WILDCARDS`, before `new RegExp(regexStr, 'i')` is ever constructed (constructing the regex is cheap; `.test()` is the cost, so refusing before construction is sufficient). Extend the module doc comment with the contract every consumer now depends on: 'returns null for a pattern it refuses; a refused pattern is to be treated as matching every string, and the caller must then keep everything rather than drop it'. Add the measured table (3/4/5/6/7 wildcards -> 8.5 ms / 105 ms / 1.02 s / 10.2 s / 84 s across 300 categories, compile <=0.06 ms throughout) and say in one line why the bound is the fix and not memoisation. Delete the trailing `// ? added here` on the escaped-wildcard branch; keep the `// escaped wildcard - treat as literal character` comment above it. Drop the `export` keyword from `REGEX_SPECIAL` (line 14), which has no consumer outside this module - keep both in-module uses on lines 25 and 35 as they are.
files.why: This is the file the ticket says the bound is defined in, and it is the only place both consumers can be made to inherit the fix. The `null` return is what makes a refusal visible to a caller instead of silently compiling the catastrophic regex.

files.change: Retype the LRU to `new LRUCache<string, RegExp | null>({ max: 500 })`. Replace `if (!cachedRegExp)` with an `=== undefined` sentinel (`let cached = likePatternCache.get(pattern); if (cached === undefined) { cached = likePatternToRegex(pattern); likePatternCache.set(pattern, cached); }`) - a cached `null` is falsy, so the existing check would recompile the pattern on every row instead of caching the refusal. After the cache lookup, `if (cached === null) return 1;` with a comment stating why a refusal returns a MATCH and not a non-match: under `$like` that returns every transaction (equal to the axis, which also keeps everything) and under `$notlike` it returns none (a strict subset of the axis), so in both directions the axis is never narrower than the result set. Do not add a second bound or a second memoisation here - the LRU already exists and the measurements show compilation is not the cost.
files.why: AC-2 requires the sqlite `UNICODE_LIKE` path to inherit the bound rather than grow a second check, so this consumer must handle `null` and no more.

files.change: Three edits. (1) `contains` branch, around line 246: hoist `const pattern = getNormalisedString('%' + condition.value + '%')` and `const matcher = likePatternToRegex(pattern)`, guard `if (typeof condition.value !== 'string') return false;` to preserve today's exact semantics, and return `matcher === null || matcher.test(getNormalisedString(textValue))`. (2) `doesNotContain` branch, around line 258: the same hoist, and return `matcher === null ? true : !matcher.test(getNormalisedString(textValue))` - a refusal must return `true` and KEEP the category, with a comment naming the trap explicitly: negating a match-everything result would drop every category, which is the money-losing direction. Both edits keep the existing comments on why the axis runs the query's two primitives, and `isSupportedCategoryCondition` already guarantees a string value, so these guards stay defensive only. (3) Drop the `export` keyword from `canNarrowAxisByConditions` (line 89; its only caller is line 137 of the same file, and the test file does not import it) and record the reason in the doc comment above it: it is unexported rather than given a direct test because all four of its branches are already covered through the only observable contract, which is `narrowCategoriesByConditions`'s - budgetDataQuery.test.ts lines 403/416 ('or' with a non-category disjunct -> gate false), 436 ('and' -> gate true), 452 (empty/undefined -> gate false) and 350 ('or' with every disjunct category-bound -> gate true) - and a second table asserting the same four outcomes through a private function would drift from the first. `matches` handling at lines 274-284 is untouched: it is not a LIKE pattern, its divergence is already axis-wider, and its 256-character test remains the precedent this ticket's length cap copies.
files.why: The axis is the money path. Both LIKE call sites must decide the refusal explicitly, and `doesNotContain` is the one that decides it the wrong way by default.

files.change: Create with YAML frontmatter `category: Bugfixes` and `authors: [Shivam-Fl]`, then a body of exactly one line and no newline in it, e.g.: 'Stop Custom and Grouped reports from freezing when a category filter value is packed with wildcard characters such as `%%%%%%`.' The release-note gate is a hard CI check and it validates adds, modifications and renames, so this file must exist for the PR to pass.

cases: Add a module-level helper `matches(pattern, value)` that calls `likePatternToRegex`, throws if it returns null, and returns `.test(value)` - then route the ~15 existing assertions through it. This is required by the type change, and it doubles as a regression suite for AC-4: every existing case (including `%%%` matching every string, `\%` reading as a literal, `_` NOT being a wildcard, and case-insensitivity) now also proves the bound refuses nothing a user would plausibly type. Do not use a non-null assertion.

New describe block 'bounds the pattern', asserting `likePatternToRegex('%'.repeat(6) + 'Z')` is null (8 unescaped wildcards) and `likePatternToRegex('%'.repeat(5))` is null - the exact 8-wildcard value AC-1 names.
Assert the boundary from both sides: a 4-wildcard pattern such as `'%' + '%%Z' + '%'` is NOT null and still matches correctly, so the cap is 4 and not 3.
Assert the count is over UNESCAPED wildcards only: a long run of backslash-escaped percent signs (`'\%'.repeat(20)`) is not refused, because it compiles to literals and adds no `.*`.
Assert the length cap independently: `'x'.repeat(257)` is null while `'x'.repeat(256)` is not, and the two numbers match the existing 256-character guard at budgetDataQuery.ts:274-278.

Assert that a refused pattern costs nothing at the call site - i.e. that no RegExp is constructed for it - by asserting the return is null rather than a RegExp; do NOT write a wall-clock timing assertion, which would be flaky in CI.

Falsifiability, required by .sdlc/memory/conventions.md: raise `MAX_UNESCAPED_WILDCARDS` to 99 in a scratch edit, record the failing run showing the 'bounds the pattern' cases go green-to-red, then revert. The test must be able to fail.
Assert `unicodeLike('%%%%%%Z', 'Food')` returns 1 - a refused pattern is a match on the query side, which is what keeps the axis from being narrower than the result set under `$like`.

Assert the refusal is cached rather than recompiled: call `unicodeLike` twice with the same refused pattern and assert the LRU holds it. Run this file under the web vitest config (`yarn workspace @actual-app/core exec vitest --run -c vitest.web.config.ts src/platform/server/sqlite/unicodeLike.test.ts`) - a bare `vitest --run` in that workspace silently skips `platform/server/sqlite/`, per .sdlc/memory/qa/environment.md. Do NOT pass `-t`, which makes the order-dependent sqlite platform tests vacuous.
Assert the pre-existing behaviour the cap must not change: `unicodeLike('%%%', 'Food')` and `unicodeLike('%?%', 'Food')` still return 1 - both are 3-wildcard patterns, under the cap.

In the 'reads text operators as LIKE patterns' describe, add the AC-3 case for `contains`: `filterBy('contains', '%%%%%%Z')` equals `allIds` (all five wildcardCategories) - a refused pattern keeps every category rather than narrowing.

Add the paired `doesNotContain` case: `filterBy('doesNotContain', '%%%%%%Z')` ALSO equals `allIds`. This is the fail-closed trap and the single most important assertion in the change - if the axis empties here, money has left every total. Add a comment saying so.

Add the boundary case in the other direction: `filterBy('contains', '%%Z')` (4 wildcards, accepted) narrows exactly as the pattern says rather than keeping everything, so a fix that made every text condition a no-op fails here.

Assert the grouped axis too, through `narrowCategoriesByConditions` rather than the helper: a `contains '%%%%%%Z'` condition returns the input BY IDENTITY (`toBe(axis)`), which is the existing contract for 'did not narrow' and is what stops the grouped array being rebuilt and empty groups deleted. This is AC-3 on the screen QA actually sees.

Re-run the existing pinned cases unchanged and say so in the commit body: `contains '%'` and `contains '?'` keep every category, `contains '\\%'` narrows to `['c-discount']`, `contains 'o%'` narrows to three, `doesNotContain '%'` is `[]`, `matches 'x'.repeat(257)` keeps every category. Any of these moving is a regression in a test that was written to catch exactly this class of change.
Falsifiability: invert the `doesNotContain` refusal to `matcher === null ? false : ...`, record the failing run, revert.

acceptance.check: The bound is enforced inside `likePatternToRegex` and no consumer re-implements it: `unicodeLike` gains no bound of its own, only a `null` check, so one change and one test cover both the report axis path and the sqlite `UNICODE_LIKE` path.

qa_script: Boot with `yarn start`, choose "Don't use a server", then "View demo" on the setup screen to get a populated budget (accounts, transactions, categories and budgeted amounts).
Open Reports -> Custom report. Note the full category list with no filter - that is the reference set for every step below.
Add a filter: field Category, operator contains, value `%%%%%%Z`. Assert the report table renders, and that the category column still shows every category from the reference set.
While that value is in place, keep typing and deleting characters in the filter field: the page stays responsive. This is the browser-observable form of 'the main thread was not blocked'.

Switch the operator to doesNotContain with the same value `%%%%%%Z`. Assert the category list is STILL the complete reference set. If it empties here, the bound is failing closed and money has left the totals - stop and file it.
Repeat steps 3 and 5 on a Grouped report. Assert every group survives, and that each group still contains all of its categories rather than only the ones that matched.

Positive controls at the cap boundary: with operator contains, value `%%Z` narrows the axis the way the pattern says (it is 4 wildcards, accepted). Value `%%%Z` is refused and keeps every category. Assert the two behave differently.

Negative controls, all of which must be unchanged from today: value `Food` narrows to the food categories; value `oo` narrows to Food only; value `%` keeps every category; value `?` keeps every category; value `\%` narrows to the one category whose name contains a literal percent sign; value `_` does NOT act as a wildcard.
Length bound: value a 40-character ordinary substring narrows normally, and a 300-character run of `x` keeps every category.
Repeat step 5 on the Grouped report's own filter, then reload the page and confirm the filter survived the reload (the report restores from sessionStorage) and the axis is still complete.

Collect console and pageerror for the whole run and assert nothing uncaught was emitted. Per .sdlc/memory/qa/environment.md both channels arrive out of band, so read them after an unconditional settle wait, and expect ordinary dev-mode noise rather than demanding silence.

Record in the QA report what the demo budget could and could not show: with a handful of categories the pre-fix multi-minute hang is not reproducible, so the timing evidence for AC-1 comes from AC-8's structural guarantee rather than from a stopwatch here.
risks: The fail-closed trap in `doesNotContain` is the one mistake this change can make, and it is silent: a refusal implemented as a match-everything regex narrows `contains` correctly while dropping every category under `doesNotContain`, so the axis becomes narrower than the query's result set and categories the query fetched lose their money from every total - the defect class PR #9 fixed. It is called out in files[], in the tests, in AC-3 and in the QA script.

Under `doesNotContain`, a refused pattern makes the query return no transactions, so that report renders empty. This is a visible degradation chosen deliberately over the alternative, which loses money silently. A person may still consider it wrong; if so it is a product decision, not a defect in this change.

Widening the return type to `RegExp | null` is a breaking change to a shared module. Both existing consumers are updated here, and TypeScript prevents a silent third, but a consumer added outside this repo would need to handle the refusal.

The `if (!cachedRegExp)` sentinel in `unicodeLike` must change to `=== undefined` in the same diff, or a cached `null` recompiles the pattern on every row - a performance regression rather than a correctness one, and the kind of thing that survives review because the tests still pass.

The cap of 4 was measured against ~45-character category names. A pathologically long category name would raise the accepted region's cost, since backtracking scales with subject length. Names are user input and bounded in practice, and this is strictly better than the unbounded behaviour it replaces.

The measurements were taken with Node's V8 regex engine on this runner; the browser ships the same engine, but the absolute milliseconds will differ from a user's machine. The shape - roughly 7x per additional wildcard - is what the cap relies on, and it holds.

No file in `forbidden_paths` is touched: the change is three source files in `packages/` plus one new file under `upcoming-release-notes/`. No new host is contacted - the app's existing reads of api.github.com and raw.githubusercontent.com are unchanged, and both are already in `env.api_allowlist`.
out_of_scope: Bounding the query-side per-transaction `matches` / `$regexp` regex in `packages/loot-core/src/server/aql/compiler.ts`, which the epic notes is already slow and is larger there. The axis's 256-character guard at budgetDataQuery.ts:274-278 is left exactly as it is; the length cap in this change copies that precedent rather than replacing it.
Routing the Sankey and Budget Analysis reports through the shared pattern - the text-operator piece, a separate ticket.

Any memoisation added to `likePatternToRegex` or to the report axis. `unicodeLike` already holds an LRU and compilation measures at <=0.06 ms, so caching cannot be the fix and no cache is added or removed.

Lowering the cap, making either constant exported, or making the bound configurable per report. The numbers are stated in the module and the measurement is recorded beside them; tuning them later is its own change.
Changing `matches` behaviour on the axis in any way, including routing it through the new bound. It is not a LIKE pattern and its divergence from the query is already axis-wider.

Removing the existing `#shared/likePattern` subpath export from `packages/loot-core/package.json`. `REGEX_SPECIAL` was reachable through it and is now not exported from the module; the subpath itself stays, because `unicodeLike` and `budgetDataQuery` both import through it.

alternatives_considered.approach: Return a match-everything RegExp (`/^[\s\S]*$/i`) for a refused pattern instead of `null`, leaving both call sites untouched.
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: It fails OPEN for `contains` and fails CLOSED for `doesNotContain`: that branch keeps a category when the regex does NOT match, so negating 'matches everything' drops every category - the axis becomes narrower than the query's result set and every category the query fetched loses its money from every total. It is the exact defect AC-3 exists to prevent, and it would have passed a `contains`-only test.

alternatives_considered.approach: Keep `likePatternToRegex` total and add a sibling `isPatternWithinBounds(pattern)` that consumers must remember to call.
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: It leaves the unbounded compile reachable - a caller that forgets the check gets the catastrophic regex with nothing to stop it, which is the hazard the ticket names when it says the bound must live inside the function. It also splits one definition of the pattern language across two exports in the file that declares itself the single definition.

alternatives_considered.approach: Throw from `likePatternToRegex` on a refused pattern and let each caller catch.
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: `unicodeLike` is a sqlite scalar function invoked per row from inside the query engine; an exception there escapes as a raw engine error rather than a fail-open result, and a per-row try/catch is the wrong shape for a control-flow signal on the hottest path in the file.

alternatives_considered.approach: Bound the value at the report UI - strip or reject wildcard characters in the Category filter field.
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: It fixes one entry point and leaves every other one unbounded: transaction rules reach the same `$like` path through `transaction-rules.ts:647`, and so does `forecast-filters.ts:235`. It also cannot satisfy AC-2, which requires the bound to live in the shared function.

alternatives_considered.approach: Fix the hang by memoising `likePatternToRegex` in the report axis.
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: The epic's measurement is right and I confirmed it: compilation is <=0.06 ms for every pattern, including the 7-wildcard one that takes 84 s to test. Caching the regex would remove 0.03% of the cost. The bound is the fix.

alternatives_considered.approach: Give `canNarrowAxisByConditions` a direct test instead of unexporting it (the other branch AC-6 allows).
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: All four of its branches are already covered through `narrowCategoriesByConditions`, its only caller and its only observable contract (budgetDataQuery.test.ts lines 403/416, 436, 452, 350). A second table asserting the same four outcomes through a private function is exactly the kind of test that drifts from the first one, and it would keep a gate that has no independent meaning exported for a future caller to depend on. The reason is recorded next to the function, as AC-6 requires.

assumptions: The wildcard count, not the pattern length, is what bounds the cost. Confirmed by measurement: a 6-character value producing an 8-wildcard pattern is where AC-1's hang lives, and no length cap below ~6 would touch it.

4 is the right cap. It keeps the accepted region at <=105 ms across 300 categories (measured), admits every value the existing pinned tests exercise (`%` and `?` compile to 3-wildcard patterns), and admits any realistic user input - no plausible category filter contains three or more unescaped wildcards.

Treating a refusal as a match on the query side (`unicodeLike` -> 1) is the correct pairing with an axis that keeps every category, because it makes the query's result set a subset of the axis in both operator directions. The alternative pairing (refusal -> 0) also satisfies the subset invariant, so the choice is made on least surprise: it makes `contains` return everything and `doesNotContain` return nothing, rather than the reverse.
`isSupportedCategoryCondition` already guarantees `typeof condition.value === 'string'` for `contains` and `doesNotContain`, so the new non-string guards are defensive and do not change behaviour.

The report axis runs synchronously in the React component body (custom-spreadsheet.ts:93, grouped-spreadsheet.ts:45), which is why the freeze is on the main thread and why the bound is worth having on this path even though the query-side UNICODE_LIKE runs in the worker.
unknowns: How much of AC-1 a QA run can actually observe. The demo budget has a handful of categories, and the pre-fix cost scales with category count and name length, so the minutes-long freeze is probably not reproducible there. AC-1 is written to what a live browser can see and AC-8 carries the falsifiable form of the same claim; if QA finds the freeze IS reproducible on the demo budget, that is worth recording in the PR.

Whether any consumer outside this repository imports `REGEX_SPECIAL`. The package's `exports` map exposes `./shared/*` as a direct file path, so the name was reachable; a repo-wide grep across packages/, scripts/, docs/ and upcoming-release-notes/ found no reference outside its own module, and this package is not published for third-party consumption as `@actual-app/core` in any configuration I could see.
validated_work_order.debate_summary: No prior plan for this issue was rejected and no decisions are recorded on its ledger, so nothing from a previous attempt constrained this one. The design question the ticket flags - which way the bound fails - resolved against the obvious implementation: the cheapest-looking fix, returning a match-everything regex, is fail-closed on `doesNotContain` and would have passed any `contains`-shaped test. The threshold was computed from a measurement taken on this runner rather than read off the epic's numbers, and the epic's figures were confirmed at the low end (3.4 ms/category at 5 wildcards against the epic's 3 ms) and found conservative at the high end.
residual_risks: If a future report grows a third LIKE consumer, the type change forces it to handle the refusal, but nothing forces it to handle it in the OPEN direction. The invariant is written into the module doc comment and asserted on both operators, so the next review has something to check against.
